accuracy.evidence: Checked against Development Matters (DfE, revised 2023), whose characteristics of effective learning list planning how to reach a goal, checking how well an activity is going, changing strategy as needed and reviewing how well the approach worked; against the EYFS statutory framework (2024) Early Learning Goal for self-regulation ('set and work towards simple goals'); and against the HighScope plan-do-review sequence. Executive function terms (working memory, inhibitory control, cognitive flexibility) follow the Harvard Center on the Developing Child definitions. No claim is stronger than the sources.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the real early-years planning slips: confusing a preference or a fact with a plan ('I like blocks', 'Cats say miaow'), starting with no plan ('Go!'), gathering every toy instead of what the plan needs (basket step and 'take them all' prediction), treating a model as finished without comparing it with the plan (no-roof prediction and missing-part step), and giving up when a material runs out (swap step).

lab_distinct.evidence: The flagplan lab is built around the plan-do-review cycle itself: speech bubbles dragged to a child, a toy shelf filtered into a basket against a stated plan, four plan cards ordered into numbered boxes, two drawn houses compared part by part with tappable roof, door and window, and material swaps judged by the job they do. None of these mechanics appear in flag_stick, flag_try or flag_swap, and the 30% shingle gate passed.

lab_teaches.evidence: The steps follow the cycle in the order a child uses it: state the goal, gather only what it needs, see the four stages in order, review the product against the plan and adapt when something runs out. Each done message names the rule the child has just used, for example 'Checking means looking back at the plan', so the text confirms what the tasks showed.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions come before the evidence: whether to take every toy (tempting yes, then the basket refuses the spoon, ball and car), when to check your work (tempting 'at the start', then the order step puts Check it last) and whether a house with no roof is done (tempting yes, then the plan picture shows the roof).

challenge_feedback.evidence: The Challenge has five questions and every wrong option carries a tag with its own message in why(): like, rush, extra, all, order, skip, quit and job. For example choosing 'Say it is done' for a door-less house gives 'Check first: look at the plan and see if a part is missing.' Lab wrong answers also name the slip, such as 'A ball rolls off. Walls need flat things that stack.'

readability.evidence: Family audience. The kid explanation scores Flesch-Kincaid -1.6 with one-syllable words and model sentences a 4-year-old can repeat ('I will build a house for Teddy'). The adult text scores 5.7, well inside the 10.0 limit, and still names the precise terms: plan-do-review, creating and thinking critically, self-regulation, executive function.

no_filler.evidence: Every kid sentence is part of the plan, get, make, check routine or a worked example of it, and every adult paragraph gives a source, a named skill, a list of common mistakes or what the lab asks. The content gate found no filler phrases, and all item prompts are unique.

mobile.evidence: Checked on 360x740 screenshots of every step before and after Show me: the speech bubbles stack full width on narrow screens, shelf cards are about 100x80 px with emoji and labels, the plan cards and both houses fit side by side, and young mode gives 56 px button twins below the canvas. Nothing is clipped; label sizes were raised after the first screenshots.

accessibility.evidence: Every drag has a button twin (each plan bubble, each shelf item 'Put blocks in the basket', each plan card, 'Missing: roof', each swap), the canvas aria-label and the live line update after every action, and wrong answers are signalled by text as well as a red outline. The browser gate runs axe in light and dark themes on desktop and iPhone 13.
